fields.v: Podivilov, A., Lomshakov, V., Savin, S., Startsev, M., Pozharskiy, R., Parshin, M., Nikolenko, S. (2026). AgentLens: Production-Assessed Trajectory Reviews for Coding Agent Evaluation. arXiv:2607.06624v2 [cs.AI], 14 Jul 2026
Preprint — arXiv:2607.06624v2 [cs.AI]; no published venue stated

Explyt (Podivilov, Lomshakov, Savin, Startsev, Pozharskiy, Parshin; industry, vendor of the Explyt AI Agent); St. Petersburg Department of the Steklov Institute of Mathematics and St. Petersburg State University (Nikolenko)

Proposes an evaluation method; secondary: Compares — AgentLens benchmark that evaluates full interactive trajectories of coding agents with formal verifiers plus LLM-judge reviews on five dimensions, a quality index, side-by-side reviews and a nightly regression pipeline; leaderboard of 17 harness/model configurations on Java tasks

No SDD approach. Harnesses: Explyt AI Agent (EAA, the authors' own IntelliJ IDEA coding assistant) and Claude Code; versions not stated. Models: Opus 4.7 (EAA; Claude Code with xhigh effort), GPT-5.5, Sonnet 4.6 (EAA and Claude Code), GLM-5.1 (self-hosted and OpenRouter), DeepSeek V4 Flash, DeepSeek V4 Pro, Haiku 4.5 (EAA and Claude Code), Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview, Gemini 3 Flash, MiniMax 2.7, Qwen 3.6 Plus, Mimo V2.5 Pro, Kimi K2.6. Judge: GPT-5.4

None prescribed by an SDD approach. Each scenario gives a task objective with a sequence of instructions and interaction steps (e.g. mandated step headers 'STARTING STEP N', approval before edits, required reports)

Scenario-defined workflows (from developer interviews and production clusters): reconnaissance, plan, approval, implementation, verification (tests/build), final report; the simulated user ends the dialog

No real human. An LLM user simulator with a persona (default: relaxed, intervenes only on clear failure; toxic: mildly frustrated; helpful available but not in the released fold) interacts with the agent and approves steps
N/A (no SDD approach); full interactive sessions run with a simulated user
Not classifiable (no specification artefact; authors do not use SDD terms)
Existing code bases (open-source Java projects matched to anonymised production-usage clusters; e.g. unit testing, legacy DB-logic migration, API documentation, bug fixes, refactors)
Released fold: 16 scenarios × 2 personas (default, toxic) = 32 trajectories per configuration; 17 configurations; repository size Not stated
Java enterprise/backend development (Spring Boot, JPA, Liquibase, Kafka, OpenAPI/Swagger), production-like coding-assistant work
N/A (no human participants in runs). Workflows obtained from interviews with programmers (number not stated) and anonymised summaries of consenting product users

Deterministic telemetry: interaction cost (price), cache hit rate, latency/agent time, generation-token throughput, generation tokens. Not in the leaderboard; reported only in examples (DeepSeek V4 Pro vs Flash: $21.20 vs $9.13, 18,987 s vs 10,973 s; Gemini 3.1 Pro total agent time 14,968 s) and 'a single run with Opus 4.7 can exceed $100'

Formal verification pass rate (scenario passes only if all verifiers pass: repository-state checks, regex checks, Maven/Gradle test execution, test coverage, build-task output, IDE static analysis); End Result LLM-judge score
None separately (IDE static-analysis 'no errors' verifier is part of formal verification)
None

LLM-judge scores (0/0.5/1 ordinal, aggregated 0-100) with written reviews: Instruction Compliance, Pitfalls, Pleasantness, Tool Calls; Quality Index = unweighted mean of five judge metrics and formal verification; tool telemetry (per-tool success rates, tool calls per chat, parallel calls); termination reason; side-by-side pairwise scores [-5..5] with p-values; Spearman correlation of QI with Artificial Analysis benchmarks

Automatic: formal verifiers and telemetry from runs in a CI pipeline (manual, nightly, weekly). LLM-as-judge: GPT-5.4 scores single trajectories for the leaderboard; pairwise judge for side-by-side. LLM judge validity rests on informal internal pairwise-annotation experiments (no formal agreement study). User simulator model not stated

Tasks: 16 Java scenarios × 2 personas (32 trajectories). Configurations: 17 harness + model pairs (EAA and Claude Code; Opus 4.7, Sonnet 4.6, Haiku 4.5 in both harnesses). Baseline: none designated (side-by-side against an anchor run in the regression pipeline). Held constant: scenarios, personas, judge GPT-5.4, high reasoning effort where supported; providers differ (official APIs, OpenRouter, self-hosted). Acceptance tests: formal verifiers (tests, repo state, regex, static analysis). Repetitions: 1 run per configuration except EAA + GLM-5.1 self-hosted (5 runs). Human intervention: none (simulated user). Bias checks: order-swap test and judge self-preference test (GPT-5.5 vs Sonnet 4.6 judges)

EAA + Opus 4.7 highest QI (81.5), then Claude Code + Opus 4.7 (76.2) and EAA + GPT-5.5 (73.0); Kimi K2.6 last (28.1) due to an OpenRouter tool-parser bug, not capability. Harness: same formal result for Opus (26 vs 26 passes) but reviews favour EAA; Claude Code + Haiku better than EAA + Haiku (63.6 vs 58.2; edit_file success 0.93 vs 0.66; Pitfalls side-by-side p = 0.038); Sonnet near tie (70.2 vs 70.1). DeepSeek V4 Flash vs Pro: QI 64.8 vs 64.1; Flash cheaper and faster ($9.13 vs $21.20, p = 0.0011; 10,973 s vs 18,987 s, p = 0.029); End Result difference not significant (p = 0.117). QI correlates most with APEX-Agents-AA (ρ = 0.82), negatively with IFBench (ρ = −0.41) and τ2-Bench Telecom (ρ = −0.25). Significance tested only in side-by-side reviews

It separated configurations and explained differences through reviews (e.g. provider bug, parallel-tool-calling regression caught nightly). Repeatability: GLM-5.1 five runs, QI mean 67.28, SD 0.94; 60.5% of QI variance from formal verification; 15 of 32 scenario-persona points passed in all runs, 1 failed in all, 16 flaky. Order-swap residuals small. Judges disagreed on the winner in 23% of task-metric comparisons (18% self-favouring, 5% opposite), half from Pleasantness; average shift ~4% of the pairwise range. Limitations stated: Java only; third-party providers outside their control; cost; benchmark built around their own assistant; judge validity not yet formally established

Limitations: specific class of coding-agent tasks, Java-only release; third-party API providers affect latency, routing, versioning and availability (leaderboard differences partly reflect serving conditions); a run can exceed $100; built around the authors' own assistant (neutrality needs external use); LLM-judge validity rests on informal internal experiments. Future work: integrations for Codex, OpenCode and more IDEs (PyCharm, Rider, WebStorm); more task folds (e.g. test writing); formal judge-human and judge-judge agreement study

Inconsistencies: §4.2 says DeepSeek V4 Pro has a 'statistically significant instruction-compliance advantage', but Appendix B gives Instruction Compliance p = 0.855 (metrics_value −0.0187). Correlation tables use n = 15 while the leaderboard has 17 rows; AA correlation uses 11 models (Kimi excluded, OpenRouter GLM used). In the extracted text the Pleasant. and Tools columns of Table 6 are detached and were assigned by row order (QI recomputes correctly, e.g. 81.5 and 54.5). Formal 81.2 = 26/32 and 87.5 = 28/32 match appendix counts. User-simulator model not stated; prices and hashes masked in example reports. Code: https://github.com/agent-lens/agent-lens-bench (open source). No pre-registration. Programming language: Java (Maven/Gradle, IntelliJ IDEA)
